# Copper Metal Service 

- Official 3-month copper prices performed strongly during the first half of August, rising from a low of $5923/t on the 4<sup>th</sup> to a peak of $6415/t on the 13<sup>th</sup> .  However, shortly after mid-month this trend was reversed with 3m quotes (3m) giving up virtually all of this gain, heading down to $5945/t on the 19<sup>th</sup> .  Subsequently, renewed impetus has seen prices driven higher, to $6400/t at the time of writing. 

- While we remain optimistic for prices in general we remain somewhat cautious about the fundamental outlook for the market in the short term.  Logic dictates that the difference between China’s apparent refined consumption growth of 48% year on year in H1 2009 and its actual consumption growth of closer to 25% must be accounted for by an increase in inventories.  At the same time, scrap availability has seen some improvement from the very low levels witnessed earlier in the year which will lead to an increase in secondary refined production as well as more scrap usage in copper’s first use and semis products (at the expense of cathodes).  Therefore, China’s cathode import requirements should be far less in H2 2009 and, in the absence of a marked pick up in demand in countries elsewhere in the world, or indeed further stock building within China, visible inventories are likely to rise further. 

- The downturn in copper demand during H1 was much stronger than we had originally anticipated for some countries. This was particularly the case with Russia and the US where we have reduced our 2009 estimates for these countries accordingly.  Overall we have reduced our global demand forecasts for this year, 2010 and 2011 by ~400kt/a and now forecast that global refined copper consumption will decline by 2.8% this year, to ~17.4Mt, before recovering by 2.4% in 2010 and 5.8% in 2011 to ~17.8Mt and ~18.8Mt respectively. 

- August has seen a reasonable uplift in the availability of spot concentrates with sales emanating from Chile, Indonesia and Peru.  There has been a fair divergence in terms which have ranged from $6/t & 0.6c/lb, to a little under $20/t & 2.0c/lb.

Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Prices were more volatile during August

** Official 3-month copper prices performed strongly during the first half of August, rising from a low of $5923/t on the 4<sup>th</sup> to a peak of $6415/t on the 13<sup>th</sup> .  However, shortly after mid-month this trend was reversed with 3m quotes (3m) giving up virtually all of this gain, heading down to $5945/t on the 19<sup>th</sup> . Subsequently, renewed impetus has seen prices driven higher, to $6400/t at the time of writing.  This is in contrast to last month where a more distinct upward trend was set, albeit at lower prices.  August trading conditions have been extremely volatile with daily min/max variations in official 3-month quotes ranging from -$340/t to +$389/t.  Prices have not been this volatile since October last year which saw the largest collapse in prices in living memory and daily min/max variations ranged from -$508/t to + $600/t. 

**Positive indicators, the threat of strike action and fresh investment money pushed prices higher** Volatile trading conditions this month have been fuelled by very mixed sentiment reflecting uncertainty amongst market participants.  On the upside, quotes were supported by the injection of fresh investment money in response to rising equity markets, the release of positive macro economic data (which raised hopes of a more imminent return to global economic growth), strike action in Canada, and the potential for further industrial action at a number of significant copper mines in Chile, Peru and North America that have forthcoming labour negotiations. 

**Macro economic data boosted sentiment** On the economic front market sentiment initially improved on the news that US pending home sales were much better than expected.  This helped propel quotes (3m) by $216/t on the 5<sup>th</sup> to $6139/t, the first time that prices had traded above $6000/t since October last year.  Sentiment strengthened further on the 13<sup>th</sup> when it was announced that GDP for France and Germany, the Eurozone’s two largest economies, increased by 0.3% during Q2 from Q1.  As a consequence, 3-month official quotes surged $389/t on the day to settle at $6415/t which represented a new 11-month high. 

**Supply disruptions add further support to the market** Various factors have contributed to the fresh inflow of investment money into the commodities complex and particularly copper.  Industrial action or the spectre of production losses on account of strike action has been a key factor.  In North America, workers at Vale Inco’s Sudbury nickel-copper mines, smelters and refineries (120kt/a Cu) have been on strike since 13<sup>th</sup> July while industrial action at the company’s Voisey’s Bay mine (40kt/a Cu) started on August 1<sup>st</sup> .  The Sudbury milling/smelting/refining facilities were closed for extended maintenance back in late May and were not due to restart until late August.  Also supporting sentiment has been the potential for additional industrial action at some of copper’s principal mines in

the countries mentioned above which, collectively, could impact ~3Mt/a of copper mine supplies (see Production). Earlier in the year these forthcoming labour negotiations were deemed to be more of a formality in terms of contract renewals given the lower price environment and the fact that many mines were in survival mode while various loss-making operations had been compelled to shut down. However, under the current higher price environment, these negotiations are likely to be far tougher with unions seeking a renewal of profit-sharing agreements along with higher wage and benefit expectations. Other positive factors have been the growing realisation that Chinese consumption is going to be far higher this year than was previously expected as well as a general belief by market participants that there are too few mine projects being developed over the next few years to meet the anticipated recovery in consumption in countries outside of China. ### **Copper LME open interest vs copper price** 265000 7000

**Copper’s forward curve steepens** The forward curve has steepened quite markedly since the end of July, reflecting a deepening backwardation in the months ahead. In fact, the recent rise in near-term prices has led to the forward curve being at its steepest at the front end of the curve (i.e. the next 44 months), indicating expectations of tightness in the market during this period. This is in contrast to the start of last month when the forward curve was in a slight contango for the next twelve months and flat thereafter. **Total exchange stock rise for the second consecutive month** Exchange stocks increased for the second consecutive month in August, rising by a net 50.5kt to 433.6kt as of the 27th . The majority of the gain reflected a net 35.5kt uplift in SHFE inventories to 86.6kt, their highest level since mid-August 2007. The rise was not surprising in light of the record level of refined imports seen in recent months alongside a seasonal decline in demand. Inventories also increased on the LME, having risen by a net 16.8kt to 299kt. Warehouses in South Korea and the US were the main recipients of this material. Inventories in Busan were up by a net 8.9kt, to 20.8kt while shipments to Chicago, New Orleans and St Louis were increased by a net 3.4kt, 5kt and 5.4kt respectively. Total LME warrants in the US, at 213kt, were at their highest since May and accounted for 71% of LME inventories overall. Elsewhere in the US, Comex copper stocks declined by a net 1.8kt to 48.1kt. **Spot activity remained extremely quiet in Europe** During the month the European physical copper market continued to experience one of its quietest summer periods on record with traders and producers reporting no improvement in orders. This surprised some traders who were expecting a small recovery in business during the latter part of the month in tandem with the return of several copper manufacturers from their summer shutdowns. As a consequence premia were unchanged from July. Thus Chilean and Grade A material continued to trade between $70-90/t while Italian warrants remained slightly higher at $90-100/t. Elsewhere, standard grade material continued to command a premium of $20-30/t as scrap availability remained limited. Metal Service Monthly – August 2009 Page 3 of 25 Copper Monthly Update **US premia remain flat** Similar to Europe, the slowdown in spot activity in

the US during the summer remained more pronounced than in previous years, according to traders. Increased scrap availability continued to impact negatively on demand. Thus premia have remained at 4-5c/lb delivered Midwest. **Chinese premia weaken in August** Chinese premia weakened further during August, falling from $80-100/t in July to $70-90/t at the time of writing. This was expected due to rising SHFE exchange stocks, reduced arbitrage opportunities and improved scrap availability. During July at least half of the 6000 container loads of scrap material (~60kt) held up in southern Chinese ports during June were moved on with the majority of the remaining containers clearing customs this month. This was highlighted by latest trade data which showed scrap imports totalling 448.3kt (gross weight) in July, up 60.7% (+169kt) from June and the highest monthly level (in tonnage terms) since October last year. However, through to July total scrap imports, at ~2.2Mt (gross weight), were down by 36.2% (-1.2Mt) year on year. **Chinese refined imports fall on a monthly basis in July** In contrast, Chinese refined copper imports surged by 168% (+1.3Mt) year on year during the first seven months of 2009. These receipts rose on a monthly basis from February through to June when a new monthly high of 379kt was recorded. However, this trend was reversed in July with imports totalling 292.2kt. Whilst this was the lowest level received since January, it was still up 232% (+204kt) from July last year. The lower level reflected reduced arbitrage opportunities during June when LME prices exceeded SHFE quotes by an average of $30/t. During July the arbitrage turned in favour of the SHFE again, but only marginally, with SHFE quotes trading an average $19/t above LME prices. Meanwhile in August, LME prices, as of the 27th, have traded an average $89/t above SHFE. Given these arbitrage movements it is very likely that refined copper imports will continue to decline during August and September. ### **Shanghai/LME arbitrage ($/t) vs refined copper imports (kt)** $/t Kt

Logic dictates that the difference between China’s apparent refined consumption growth of 48% year on year in H1 2009 and its actual consumption growth of closer to 25% must be accounted for by an increase in inventories. Therefore, China’s cathode import requirements should be far less in H2 2009 and, in the absence of a marked pick up in demand in countries elsewhere in the world, or indeed further stock building within China, visible inventories are likely to rise further. That said a potentially large proportion of this is likely to remain in China and we have thus kept our 2009 price forecasts broadly unchanged from last month at $4841/t ($2.20/lb). **We have increased our market surplus for 2010** We see no lack of additional mine supply in 2010 with output rising by more than 1Mt based upon higher contributions from operations such as Los Pelambres (+120kt), Collahuasi (+100kt), Escondida (+80kt), Andacollo (+70kt), Lumwana (+65kt), Chuqui (+55kt), Tenke (+45kt), Konkola Deep (+45kt) etc. This, coupled with the knock-on effect of the large revision made to our 2009 demand estimates, has raised our global surplus projection for 2010 to ~650kt and we now forecast that average prices will decline by 4.5% next year to $4625/t ($2.10/lb). However, in 2011 market conditions are expected to improve, in line with a global recovery in demand, which is reflected in our average price forecast of $5075/t ($2.30/lb) and an essentially balanced market. Metal Service Monthly – August 2009 Page 6 of 25 Copper Monthly Update ## Economic Developments **Japan exits recession, aided by improving terms of trade** Japan’s economy started growing again during the second quarter, following the sharp contraction earlier in the year that pushed output back to 2004 levels. Real GDP expanded by 0.9% quarter on quarter, due largely to a pick-up in net exports, deriving more from an improvement in Japan’s terms of trade rather than a significant improvement in consumer demand abroad. Net exports contributed 1.6% towards the economic growth in the quarter, and were up by an impressive 84.7% on a seasonally adjusted basis from the preceding quarter. Subsidies for environmentally friendly cars in the US and Europe helped boost vehicle exports. Japan’s trade balance is expected to improve further in the coming months, as shipments to Asia have been steadily strengthening in recent months, but we remain cautious about the prospects of a recovery in export demand with key trading partners outside of Asia in particular. **Domestic demand continues to look fragile, and could pull Japan back into recession** While Japan’s external economy has improved, the domestic economy continues to be very weak. Domestic consumption contracted by 0.7% in April to June from the preceding quarter. The largest drag on the economy has been investment. The rate of co

ntraction in housing starts accelerated once more in June, reaching -32.4% from a year earlier. Machinery orders were down by 41.1% in June, a slight improvement over the previous month, but the survey of producers shows that core orders are expected to fall a further 8.6% in July to September from the second quarter of 2009, consistent with other indicators and suggesting that Japanese firms will continue to slash investment spending in 2010. Private consumption in Japan was boosted somewhat by the government’s fiscal stimulus, but the effects of the package appear to be waning, with supermarket sales in July declining by 4.8%, compared with -4.4% in June, and reversing the slowdown in the rate of contraction that had been taking place since February. With stimulus effects fading, unemployment rising, and investment still contracting, it is not yet clear whether Japan can stay clear of recession over the coming year. ### **Japan housing starts and machinery orders** 50

Exports in July, although still down by 20% from a year earlier, have rebounded by 55% from the January low which, coupled with the very low import levels, has resulted in the past four months being the four largest trade surpluses on record. Consumer spending and fixed-asset investment expanded through the second quarter, and households are increasingly positive over spending plans. ## Consumption 

**Global IP improving, but metals demand lags** Evidence has emerged to suggest that demand prospects outside of China are improving.  This follows the latest set of OECD lead indicators for June which implied an improved outlook for developed world industrial production (IP).  For the OECD as a whole, the 12-month rate of change in IP rose from -10.3% in February this year to -6.1% recently.  The EU lead indicator recorded the biggest improvement, rising from -9.7% in February to -3.2% in June.  The latest set of Purchasing Manager’s Indices (PMI’s) was also encouraging, with several significant indicators reaching above 50, thereby indicating growth. 

Despite the brighter outlook, however, latest data available specifically regarding metals showed that the downturn in copper demand during H1 was much stronger that we had originally anticipated for some countries.  This was particularly the case with Russia and the US where we have reduced our 2009 estimates for these countries by 287kt and 56kt respectively.  Elsewhere, we have made some minor revisions (Italy, Malaysia and Poland) which resulted in a reduction of our global demand forecasts for this year, 2010 and 2011 by ~400kt/a overall.  Thus we now forecast that global refined copper consumption will decline by 2.8% this year, to ~17.4Mt, before recovering by 2.4% in 2010 and 5.8% in 2011 to ~17.8Mt and ~18.8Mt respectively. 

**Russian exports of cathode surge during H1** The weaker than expected demand for cathode in Russia reflected a change in duty policy rather than the general slowdown in global demand.  Previously we noted that in recent years the Russians produced excessive amounts of copper wire rod for the export market to avoid the 10% duty on cathode exports.  We saw this last year when Russian copper wire rod exports increased by 36.6% (+119.3kt).  However, in April this year the 10% export duty on cathodes was abolished and, as a result, domestic copper producers have preferred to export their cathode rather than convert it into copper wire rod.  As a consequence copper wire rod exports declined by 64% in Q1 from 119.3kt to 43.3kt, according to latest trade date.  Meanwhile indicative data showed cathode exports rising from 92kt in H1 last year to 213kt in H1 this year, up 131.5%.  At the same time, refined production during the first six months of the year was broadly unchanged, implying that apparent refined copper consumption declined by ~40%. This is possible because copper wire rod exports account for more than half of the country’s refined copper consumption. Thus we have revised our Russian refined copper demand estimates for this year to reflect this and now forecast that Russian refined copper consumption will decline by 41.6% this year, down from 685kt last year to 4

00kt. 

**US demand for copper much lower than expected during H1** The extent of the slowdown in US refined copper demand during H1 was highlighted recently by data released by the American Bureau of Metal Statistics (ABMS). According to the Association the consumption of cathode by the copper wire rod producers declined by ~26% (-205kt) through to June from a year earlier.  By the same token we estimate that cathode consumed by the brass mills also fell by ~26% (-77kt) year on year during H1.  Demand generally continued to be impacted by the downturn in both the construction and auto sectors.  As a consequence Wolverine Tube recently reported a 29.2% (-6.2kt) decline in shipments of copper tube during Q2 from a year earlier.  The company cited a decline in demand from the heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) and electrical appliance markets as the primary reason for the fall.  For H1, overall, the company’s shipments of copper tube were down 27% (-25.5kt) from the corresponding period in 2008.  This is line with the industry as a whole, and is reflected in the ABMS data which show a 27% (-46.4kt) year on year decline in copper tube shipments during the first five months of the year.  Shipments of copper products, overall, declined by 28.6% year on year (-81kt) through to May while deliveries of copper alloy products fell by a larger 38.2% (-100kt) annually during the same 5-month period. 

**US housing sector bottoming out** On a slightly positive note the US housing sector appears to have reached bottom. In July housing starts slipped by 1% month on month to a seasonally adjusted annualized rate of 581,000 units which is still within the 500,000-600,000 range that has been seen for much of this year.  This sustained period of low activity (housing starts this year have been 40-50% lower than they were 12 months ago) has helped in the depletion of inventories of new homes.  However, with still high numbers of foreclosures, total US housing inventories remain at elevated levels and its extremely unlikely that the pace of housing starts will increase in the near term. 

**Public sector boosts non-residential construction** Non-residential construction is also showing some signs of stability.  Private sector non-residential spending in June was at a seasonally-adjusted annual rate of $397.9Bn, down by 4.8% in year on year terms and down 0.5% in month on month terms.  The public sector spending rate was $321.7Bn, a year on year rise of 5.1% and up by 1% in month on month terms, the first such monthly increase since March and a result of the funds that are starting to be spent because of the US stimulus programmes. **Codelco raises Q2 output by 22.4%** Codelco, the world’s largest copper producer has seen a 22.4% year-on-year increase in its Q2 production, from 352.8kt to 432kt Cu.  At the Nortй division production was 214.9kt in the April-June 2009 period (compared with 196.6kt a year earlier).  Elsewhere, output at Salvador was 15.5kt (10.9kt), Andina 51.4kt (46.8kt), El Teniente 98.9kt (73.5kt) and Gaby 31.1kt (4.3kt).  Codelco’s 49% share of El Abra production added a further 20.2kt (20.7kt).  Note that these production figures relate to commercial production (cathodes, blister/anodes and copperin-concentrates) and hence they are a hybrid of metal contained and recoverable copper.  The state copper company has submitted an EIS for a new SxEw mine at its Salvador division which it hopes to bring into production in H2 2012. The $220M San Antonio project hosts 170Mt of oxide reserves grading 0.52% Cu and is projected to produce 30kt/a Cu over its 20-year mine life.  The Salvador underground mine is due to close in 2011.

**Escondida’s Laguna Seca SAG mill restart achieved ahead of schedule** Repairs to Escondida’s Laguna Seca SAG mill were completed well ahead of schedule with the operation being restarted on August 2<sup>nd</sup> .  The company had expected the rewiring and coil replacement etc. to take 45 days whereas, in the event, lost production amounted to just 33 days. 

**Teck Mining announces potential commissioning delays at its Andacollo project** Teck Mining has announced that challenges to the previously granted permits for the water supply arrangements for its Andacollo copper project may result in delays to the start-up of the project.  Teck is in dialogue with national and regional authorities to resolve the issue and has contingency plans for alternate water supply which it is now proceeding with in case these become necessary.  Given the status of the relevant permits, the company believes that there is now a risk that start-up of the project will be delayed beyond the current target for first ore through the mill of November 2009. The length of any delay will depend on the outcome of discussions with authorities and the nature of required changes to Andacollo's water system, if any.  The Andacollo project, located in Chile, is scheduled to produce 75-80kt/a of copper-in-concentrates. 

**Israeli copper project gets new lease of life** It appears that the Timna SxEw project in Israel has been given a new lease of life after the country’s Industry and Trade Ministry gave approval for a government grant covering $35M of the overall project investment (originally estimated to be $175M).  In August 2008 Mexico’s AHMSA suspended development work after it received notification that it would not be receiving the grant.  This latest news means that, subject to all permit approvals, the 18 month programme of mine development and plant construction effectively now has the green light to proceed.  The project is located near Eilat in the south of the country and the plan would be to exploit underground ores, grading 1.2% Cu via room and pillar and then to recover copper via heap leaching and SxEw.  Initial plans call for a stage I project capacity of 22kt/a Cu, rising to 40kt/a Cu in stage II. 

**Mitsubishi Materials restores production to full capacity at its Naoshima and Onahama smelters** Mitsubishi Materials has raised the operating rates of its Naoshima and its 51%-owned Onahama copper smelters to full capacity after having instigated production cuts in February 2009.  The company initiated 10% cuts to both plants at the start of the year in response

to low TC/RCs and lacklustre demand for metal. In addition, in mid March a fire at the Onahama smelter led to the decision to reduce output to 65% of capacity while repairs were carried out. These have since been completed and the company now aims to meet its target of producing 24.3kt/m of metal for the April through September period. In 2008 Naoshima produced 220kt of refined copper while Onahama’s cathode output (including anodes refined on behalf of Naoshima) was 240kt Cu. **RTB Bor plans to raise mine production** Serbia’s sole copper producer, RTB Bor plans to raise copper-in-concentrate output from its own mines from just 16kt last year, to 80kt within the next seven years. At the Veliki Krivelj mine production will be increased from 10kt/a to 25kt/a while at Majdanpek production should peak at 20kt/a from the current rate of 5kt/a. In another development the Cerovo pit, which was last operated in 2002, will be reopened in 2013 with production rising there to 25kt/a. There are no expansion plans for the Bor underground mine which has limited reserves. Within the Bor smelter only one of the two reverberatory furnaces is presently in operation, limiting capacity to 70kt/a. That said the Bor copper smelter/refinery produced only 33.75kt of refined copper last year from the company’s own mines and from imported feed, primarily from Bulgaria and to a much lesser extent, Romania.
